name_khmer: នំអន្សមចេក
name_english: Num Ansorm Chek — banana sticky rice cake
context: Festival (Pchum Ben, Khmer New Year) / Religious ceremony
description:
A steamed cake of glutinous rice, sweet baby banana and rich coconut milk wrapped tightly in banana leaves. It is one of the most culturally significant items in Cambodian culinary heritage, woven into major ancestral and religious observances.

The outer layer of glutinous rice is soft, chewy and rich from coconut cream, balanced by the fragrant sweetness of ripe chek nam wa (baby bananas) at the core, which turn a deep reddish-purple during the long steaming.

INGREDIENTS
Glutinous rice, ripe baby bananas (chek nam wa), fresh coconut milk, sugar, salt, fresh banana leaves, split bamboo string or raffia.

PREPARATION
Glutinous rice is soaked, washed and seasoned with coconut milk, salt and sugar. Bananas are peeled and placed in the centre of rice laid flat on wilted banana leaves. The leaf is rolled tightly into a dense cylinder, tucked at both ends and bound firmly with bamboo string. The logs are boiled continuously for six to eight hours.

REGION
Nationwide — Battambang, Siem Reap and the rural agrarian heartlands.

NOTE
The cylindrical shape is a traditional symbol of unity, strength and agricultural abundance, offered to monks and ancestors.

name_english: Num Korm — palm sugar and coconut filled rice dumpling
description:
A delicate, pyramid-shaped steamed dumpling of glutinous rice flour dough enclosing a sweet, aromatic filling of fresh grated coconut cooked with dark palm sugar.

The outer rice flour skin is soft and pliable against the rich, chewy interior. Toasted sesame seeds in the filling lend a warm, nutty aroma that defines traditional Khmer confectionery technique.

INGREDIENTS
Glutinous rice flour, water, Kampong Speu palm sugar (skor tnot), freshly grated coconut, toasted white sesame seeds, banana leaves cut into triangles, coconut oil or lard for brushing.

PREPARATION
Glutinous rice flour is kneaded with water into a smooth dough. The filling is cooked down by caramelising palm sugar with fresh coconut and sesame seeds. Portioned dough balls are flattened, stuffed, wrapped into precise pyramidal parcels using oiled banana leaves, and steamed for 20 to 25 minutes.

REGION
Kandal, Kampong Cham, and nationwide.

NOTE
The pyramid structure echoes the sacred stupas and architectural geometries found across ancient Khmer stone temples.

name_khmer: នំអន្សមជ្រូក
name_english: Num Ansorm Chrouk — savoury pork and mung bean sticky rice cake
context: Festival (Pchum Ben, Khmer New Year) / Special occasion
description:
The savoury counterpart to Num Ansorm Chek: glutinous rice layered with seasoned split yellow mung beans and a central strip of black-pepper-marinated pork belly, steamed in banana leaf cylinders.

Fat from the pork belly melts into the mung beans and rice during the long boil, giving a rich, savoury dumpling with a pungency from crushed Kampot black pepper.

INGREDIENTS
Glutinous rice, split yellow mung beans (soaked and hulled), pork belly in thick strips, black pepper, garlic, sea salt, fresh banana leaves, bamboo string.

PREPARATION
Rice is seasoned and layered over banana leaves, followed by steamed mung beans and pork belly strips marinated in pepper and salt. Wrapped into heavy cylindrical logs, bound tightly, and boiled for six to eight hours. Leftovers are sliced into thick wheels and pan-fried until golden and crisp.

REGION
Kampong Speu, Battambang, and nationwide.

NOTE
Illustrates the historic technique of preserving high-value meat cuts within a fat and rice medium for extended festival celebrations.

name_english: Num Plae Ai — palm sugar sticky rice balls with fresh coconut
description:
Small, bouncy glutinous rice dumplings stuffed with a solid cube of hard palm sugar, boiled until cooked, then rolled in freshly shaved coconut.

The texture is springy and soft. Biting into a warm dumpling bursts the melted palm sugar inside, against the cool, savoury grated coconut outside.

INGREDIENTS
Glutinous rice flour, warm water, hard palm sugar cubes, freshly grated coconut, a pinch of sea salt.

PREPARATION
The dough is divided into small balls, hollowed with a thumb, stuffed with a palm sugar cube and sealed tightly. The balls are dropped into boiling water; once they float they are moved straight into cold water, then rolled in grated coconut mixed with sea salt.

REGION
Takeo, Phnom Penh, and nationwide.

NOTE
Folklore names this one num samlap pdei, the husband-killing cake — a warning never to eat one in a single warm bite, in case the hot liquid palm sugar squirts out. A street snack beloved for its short ingredient list and its play on temperature and texture.

name_english: Num Kong — crispy fried rice-flour donuts with palm sugar glaze
context: Daily life / Afternoon tea / Market snack
description:
Traditional fried donuts made from rice flour and glutinous rice flour, shaped into rings, deep-fried until golden and coated with caramelised palm sugar and toasted sesame seeds.

A crunchy golden shell over a tender, chewy interior. The dark palm sugar glaze adds a deep caramel flavour lifted by the nutty aroma of white sesame.

INGREDIENTS
Rice flour, glutinous rice flour, warm water, palm sugar syrup, white sesame seeds, oil for deep frying.

PREPARATION
The flours are mixed with warm water into a pliable dough, rolled into small ropes and looped into rings. They are fried until puffed and crisp. Palm sugar is caramelised separately into a thick glaze, drizzled over the donuts and finished with toasted sesame seeds.

REGION
Siem Reap, Kampong Chhnang, and market towns.

NOTE
Reflects everyday Cambodian market culture and a deep-frying tradition built on rice rather than wheat. Sold in the late afternoon by street vendors, wrapped in fresh lotus leaf.

name_english: Num Kor — steamed palm sugar cake topped with coconut
context: Special occasion / Seasonal harvest / Daily life
description:
A light, airy steamed cake of rice flour, fragrant palm fruit pulp (tnot) and palm sugar, a vibrant orange-yellow crowned with fresh salted shredded coconut.

Spongy, soft and moist, with a sweet, floral aroma that comes straight from mature palmyra palm fruit and unrefined palm sugar.

INGREDIENTS
Rice flour, mature toddy palm fruit pulp (tnot), unrefined palm sugar, coconut cream, a fermented rice starter or yeast, freshly shredded coconut, a pinch of salt.

PREPARATION
Rice flour is mixed with extracted palm fruit pulp, palm sugar and coconut cream, then left to ferment slightly for airiness. The batter is poured into small leaf cups or metal ramekins, steamed over high heat until risen and spongy, and sprinkled with salted grated coconut.

REGION
Kampong Speu and Takeo — the palm sugar producing heartlands.

NOTE
Shows the culinary use of Borassus flabellifer, the palmyra palm and Cambodia's national tree, drawing on both the fruit pulp and the tree sap. Made in the dry season, when fresh toddy palm syrup comes in from the fields.

name_english: Num Bot — folded mung bean glutinous rice dumpling
description:
A folded dumpling of sweet mung bean paste enclosed in glutinous rice dough, wrapped into neat, flat rectangular banana leaf packets rather than rolled or tied.

The texture is delicate and smooth: a rich, sweet mung bean interior infused with coconut inside soft rice dough.

INGREDIENTS
Glutinous rice flour, hulled split yellow mung beans, coconut cream, white sugar, salt, softened banana leaves.

PREPARATION
Mung beans are steamed, mashed and cooked down with coconut cream and sugar until thick. Small balls of bean paste are enveloped in glutinous rice dough, placed onto flat banana leaf sheets, folded into neat flat rectangles — bot means to fold — and steamed until glossy.

REGION
Battambang and Prey Veng.

NOTE
Rare today. Where Num Korm remains widely available, Num Bot with its flat fold geometry has largely gone from urban markets and survives in select rural communities. It demonstrates a specialised banana-leaf wrapping art that depends on folding rather than string-tying.
